claim: O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic post-translational modification that diversifies the proteome.
source: O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic post-translational modification that diversifies the proteome.
evidence: This is a general statement about O-GlcNAcylation that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Dysregulation of O-GlcNAcylation is associated with neurological disorders that impair cognitive function.
source: Its dysregulation is associated with neurological disorders that impair cognitive function
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature throughout the manuscript and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The authors developed an O-GlcNAcylation profiling tool that combines O-GlcNAc binding activity from CpOGA with TurboID proximity labeling in Drosophila.
source: By combining an O-GlcNAc binding activity derived from Clostridium perfringens OGA (CpOGA) with TurboID proximity labeling in Drosophila, we developed an O-GlcNAcylation profiling tool that translates O-GlcNAc modification into biotin conjugation for tissue-specific candidate substrates enrichment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing the development and validation of the tool.

claim: Components of the translational machinery, particularly ribosomal subunits, were abundantly O-GlcNAcylated in the mushroom body of Drosophila brain.
source: We mapped the O-GlcNAc interactome in major brain regions of Drosophila and found that components of the translational machinery, particularly ribosomal subunits, were abundantly O-GlcNAcylated in the mushroom body of Drosophila brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and GO enrichment analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation induced by ectopic expression of active CpOGA in the mushroom body decreased local translational activity.
source: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation induced by ectopic expression of active CpOGA in the mushroom body decreased local translational activity, leading to olfactory learning deficits that could be rescued by dMyc overexpression-induced increase of protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by OPP protein synthesis assay data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation in the mushroom body leads to olfactory learning deficits.
source: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation induced by ectopic expression of active CpOGA in the mushroom body decreased local translational activity, leading to olfactory learning deficits that could be rescued by dMyc overexpression-induced increase of protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral learning assay data presented in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: dMyc overexpression-induced increase of protein synthesis can rescue olfactory learning deficits caused by hypo-O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation induced by ectopic expression of active CpOGA in the mushroom body decreased local translational activity, leading to olfactory learning deficits that could be rescued by dMyc overexpression-induced increase of protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation involves reversible attachment of β-N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) to the hydroxyl group of serine and threonine residues of protein substrates.
source: It involves reversible attachment of β-N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) to the hydroxyl group of serine and threonine residues of protein substrates, catalyzed by a pair of evolutionarily conserved enzymes, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA) (Vocadlo, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vocadlo, 2012 and represents established knowledge.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is catalyzed by a pair of evolutionarily conserved enzymes, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA).
source: It involves reversible attachment of β-N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) to the hydroxyl group of serine and threonine residues of protein substrates, catalyzed by a pair of evolutionarily conserved enzymes, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA) (Vocadlo, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vocadlo, 2012 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The addition and removal of O-GlcNAc moiety are dynamic, with cycling rates ranging from several minutes to the lifetime of a protein.
source: As a monosaccharide modification, the addition and removal of O-GlcNAc moiety are dynamic, with cycling rates ranging from several minutes to the lifetime of a protein (Miller et al., 1999; Roquemore et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Miller et al., 1999 and Roquemore et al., 1996.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation exerts critical regulatory functions in transcription, translation, and protein homeostasis.
source: By modifying different protein substrates, O-GlcNAcylation exerts critical regulatory functions in a wide range of basic cellular processes, including transcription, translation, and protein homeostasis (Yang and Qian, 2017; Uygar and Lagerlöf, 2023; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yang and Qian, 2017; Uygar and Lagerlöf, 2023; Wang et al., 2023.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is ubiquitously distributed but more abundant in some tissues, such as the brain.
source: O-GlcNAcylation is ubiquitously distributed but more abundant in some tissues, such as the brain (Fehl and Hanover, 2022; Wulff-Fuentes et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fehl and Hanover, 2022 and Wulff-Fuentes et al., 2021.

claim: O-GlcNAc cycling is required for the development and functions of central nervous system.
source: Given its enrichment in brain tissues and essential biological functions, it is not surprising that O-GlcNAc cycling is required for the development and functions of central nervous system (Olivier-Van Stichelen and Hanover, 2015; Lagerlöf, 2018; Akan et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Olivier-Van Stichelen and Hanover, 2015; Lagerlöf, 2018; Akan et al., 2018.

claim: Dysregulation of O-GlcNAcylation is linked to numerous neurological disorders.
source: its dysregulation is linked to numerous neurological disorders (Uygar and Lagerlöf, 2023; Lagerlöf, 2018; Lee et al., 2021; Banerjee et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Uygar and Lagerlöf, 2023; Lagerlöf, 2018; Lee et al., 2021; Banerjee et al., 2016.

claim: Hypomorphic mutations of OGT are implicated in an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome.
source: Hypomorphic mutations of OGT are implicated in an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome (Pravata et al., 2020a; Pravata et al., 2019; Selvan et al., 2018; Willems et al., 2017; Vaidyanathan et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pravata et al., 2020a; Pravata et al., 2019; Selvan et al., 2018; Willems et al., 2017; Vaidyanathan et al., 2017.

claim: The X-linked intellectual disability syndrome caused by OGT mutations is now termed OGT-associated Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation (OGT-CDG).
source: a severe neurodevelopmental disorder now termed OGT-associated Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation (OGT-CDG) (Pravata et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pravata et al., 2020b.

claim: Drosophila models of OGT-CDG that carry the equivalent human disease-related OGT missense mutations manifest deficits in sleep and habituation.
source: Drosophila models of OGT-CDG that carry the equivalent human disease-related OGT missense mutations manifest deficits in sleep and habituation, an evolutionarily conserved form of non-associative learning (Fenckova et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fenckova et al., 2022.

claim: Decreased O-GlcNAcylation level in Drosophila, induced through overexpression of CpOGA, leads to a deficit of associative olfactory learning.
source: Our recent work has shown that decreased O-GlcNAcylation level in Drosophila, induced through overexpression of a bacterial OGA from Clostridium perfringens (CpOGA), leads to a deficit of associative olfactory learning.
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' recent work and is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: Ectopic expression of CpOGA during early embryogenesis results in reduced brain size and learning defects in adult flies.
source: More interestingly, ectopic expression of CpOGA during early embryogenesis results in reduced brain size and learning defects in adult flies, likely due to interference of the sog-Dpp signaling required for neuroectoderm specification (Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2023.

claim: Disturbed O-GlcNAc homeostasis can impact cognitive function by compromising neuronal development.
source: These studies reveal that disturbed O-GlcNAc homeostasis can impact cognitive function by compromising neuronal development.
evidence: This statement is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: Impaired O-GlcNAcylation is implicated in aging-related neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: On the other hand, a number of studies have revealed that impaired O-GlcNAcylation is implicated in aging-related neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD ) (Uygar and Lagerlöf, 2023; Lagerlöf, 2018; Lee et al., 2021; Banerjee et al., 2016; Balana and Pratt, 2021; Quan et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Uygar and Lagerlöf, 2023; Lagerlöf, 2018; Lee et al., 2021; Banerjee et al., 2016; Balana and Pratt, 2021; Quan et al., 2023.

claim: In the cerebrum of AD patients, O-GlcNAcylation levels are significantly lower than that of healthy controls.
source: In the cerebrum of AD patients, O-GlcNAcylation levels are significantly lower than that of healthy controls (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2009.

claim: Upregulation of O-GlcNAcylation levels by limiting OGA activity recovers the impaired cognitive function in AD mice models.
source: Upregulation of O-GlcNAcylation levels by limiting OGA activity recovers the impaired cognitive function in AD mice models (Park et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Park et al., 2021 and Kim et al., 2013.

claim: During normal aging in mice, reduction of O-GlcNAcylation levels occurs in the hippocampus.
source: Interestingly, during normal aging in mice, reduction of O-GlcNAcylation levels also occurs in the hippocampus, and elevation of neuronal O-GlcNAc modification ameliorates associative learning and memory (Wheatley et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wheatley et al., 2019.

claim: Elevation of neuronal O-GlcNAc modification ameliorates associative learning and memory in aging mice.
source: Interestingly, during normal aging in mice, reduction of O-GlcNAcylation levels also occurs in the hippocampus, and elevation of neuronal O-GlcNAc modification ameliorates associative learning and memory (Wheatley et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wheatley et al., 2019.

claim: O-GlcNAc homeostasis is required for normal neuronal activity and cognitive function.
source: These results indicate that, in addition to its involvement in neurodevelopment, O-GlcNAc homeostasis is also required for normal neuronal activity and cognitive function.
evidence: This statement is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: The identity of key O-GlcNAc protein substrates supporting cognitive abilities in adult brain and their spatial distribution remain largely unknown.
source: However, the identity of key O-GlcNAc protein substrates supporting the cognitive abilities in adult brain and their spatial distribution remain largely unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Enrichment of O-GlcNAc-modified proteins is required for mass spectrometry (MS)-based profiling of O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Given the structural diversity and relatively low abundance, enrichment of O-GlcNAc-modified proteins is required for mass spectrometry (MS)-based profiling of O-GlcNAcylation (Yin et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yin et al., 2021 and represents established knowledge.

claim: O-GlcNAc antibodies including RL2 and CTD110.6, as well as O-GlcNAc-binding lectins such as wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), are commonly used for enrichment.
source: O-GlcNAc antibodies including RL2 and CTD110.6, as well as O-GlcNAc-binding lectins such as wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), are commonly used for enrichment.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about common methods in the field.

claim: The catalytic-dead mutant of CpOGA that retains the ability to recognize O-GlcNAcylated substrates was successfully repurposed to concentrate many developmental regulators from Drosophila embryo lysates.
source: In addition, the catalytic-dead mutant of CpOGA that retains the ability to recognize O-GlcNAcylated substrates was successfully repurposed to concentrate many developmental regulators from Drosophila embryo lysates (Selvan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Selvan et al., 2017.

claim: A recent study coupled the O-GlcNAc-binding lectin GafD to the proximity labeling TurboID yielding the GlycoID tool.
source: A recent study coupled the O-GlcNAc-binding lectin GafD to the proximity labeling TurboID yielding the GlycoID tool (Liu et al., 2022)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: TurboID enzyme attaches nonhydrolyzable biotin tags to proximal proteins within approximately 10 nm radius.
source: in which GafD domain recognizes O-GlcNAcylated substrates and the TurboID enzyme attaches nonhydrolyzable biotin tags to proximal proteins within approximately 10 nm radius (Branon et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Branon et al., 2018.

claim: The GlycoID tool was used to profile O-GlcNAcylation in different subcellular spaces including the nucleus and cytosol.
source: The GlycoID tool was used to profile O-GlcNAcylation in different subcellular spaces including the nucleus and cytosol (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: The O-GlcNAcylated proteins identified by different O-GlcNAcylation profiling strategies are quite diverse, probably due to the dynamic nature of O-GlcNAc cycling as well as the potential bias in substrates preference intrinsic to the methods.
source: It is noteworthy that the O-GlcNAcylated proteins identified by different O-GlcNAcylation profiling strategies are quite diverse, probably due to the dynamic nature of O-GlcNAc cycling as well as the potential bias in substrates preference intrinsic to the methods (Zachara et al., 2004; Ma and Hart, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zachara et al., 2004 and Ma and Hart, 2014, and includes speculation about the reasons for diversity.

claim: None of the existing O-GlcNAcylation profiling methods has been adopted for tissue-specific identification of O-GlcNAcylated proteins.
source: However, none of them has been adopted for tissue-specific identification of O-GlcNAcylated proteins.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in existing methods.

claim: Ectopic expression of CpOGA in the mushroom body reduced local O-GlcNAcylation levels and impaired olfactory learning.
source: Ectopic expression of CpOGA in the major learning center of Drosophila brain, the mushroom body, reduced local O-GlcNAcylation levels and impaired olfactory learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 1E, and 1F.

claim: The mushroom body is the major learning center of Drosophila brain.
source: Ectopic expression of CpOGA in the major learning center of Drosophila brain, the mushroom body, reduced local O-GlcNAcylation levels and impaired olfactory learning.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about Drosophila neurobiology.

claim: The authors generated an O-GlcNAc atlas for different brain regions of Drosophila (tsOGA, https://www.kyuanlab.com/tsOGA).
source: By conditional expression of this tool to translate O-GlcNAc modification into biotin conjugation in specific brain structures, we mapped the O-GlcNAc interactome and generated an O-GlcNAc atlas for different brain regions of Drosophila (tsOGA, https://www.kyuanlab.com/tsOGA).
evidence: This claim is supported by the creation of the online database described in the manuscript.

claim: Lowering the mushroom body O-GlcNAcylation levels reduced the synthesis of new proteins.
source: Lowering the mushroom body O-GlcNAcylation levels reduced the synthesis of new proteins, interfering with olfactory learning, which could be reversed by increasing ribosomal biogenesis via overexpression of dMyc.
evidence: This claim is supported by OPP assay data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Reduced protein synthesis in the mushroom body interferes with olfactory learning.
source: Lowering the mushroom body O-GlcNAcylation levels reduced the synthesis of new proteins, interfering with olfactory learning, which could be reversed by increasing ribosomal biogenesis via overexpression of dMyc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and protein synthesis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Increasing ribosomal biogenesis via overexpression of dMyc can reverse the olfactory learning deficits caused by lowered O-GlcNAcylation.
source: Lowering the mushroom body O-GlcNAcylation levels reduced the synthesis of new proteins, interfering with olfactory learning, which could be reversed by increasing ribosomal biogenesis via overexpression of dMyc.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Compromised translational activity in the brain learning center contributes to the cognitive deficits of O-GlcNAcylation insufficiency-associated neurological diseases.
source: We propose that compromised translational activity in the brain learning center contributes to the cognitive deficits of O-GlcNAcylation insufficiency-associated neurological diseases.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Elav-Gal4 induced CpOGAWT expression in the whole brain.
source: As expected, Elav-Gal4 induced CpOGAWT expression in the whole brain (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Elav-Gal4 driven CpOGAWT expression led to decreased O-GlcNAcylation levels compared to CpOGADM.
source: As expected, Elav-Gal4 induced CpOGAWT expression in the whole brain (Figure 1B), leading to decreased O-GlcNAcylation levels compared to the CpOGADM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: OK107-Gal4 drove CpOGAWT expression in the mushroom body and downregulated O-GlcNAcylation levels in the Kenyon cells.
source: For instance, OK107-Gal4 drove CpOGAWT expression in the mushroom body and downregulated O-GlcNAcylation levels in the Kenyon cells (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Conditional expression of CpOGAWT in brain neurons or mushroom body compromised the ability to establish the association between odor and electric shock.
source: Compared to CpOGADM, conditional expression of CpOGAWT in brain neurons or mushroom body compromised the ability to establish the association between odor and electric shock (Figure 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral learning assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Flies expressing CpOGAWT or CpOGADM in the ellipsoid body showed no statistical difference in learning performance.
source: In contrast, flies expressing CpOGAWT or CpOGADM in the ellipsoid body, as well as the control flies without a Gal4 driver, showed no statistical difference in the learning performance (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral learning assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Temporally controlled expression of CpOGAWT specifically in the adult mushroom body did not affect odor acuity but significantly disrupted olfactory learning relative to CpOGADM control.
source: This temporally controlled expression of CpOGAWT specifically in the adult mushroom body did not affect the odor acuity but significantly disrupted olfactory learning relative to CpOGADM control (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Proper O-GlcNAcylation homeostasis is essential for the mushroom body function.
source: These results suggested that proper O-GlcNAcylation homeostasis is essential for the mushroom body function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing learning deficits when O-GlcNAcylation is perturbed in the mushroom body.

claim: The mushroom body is the associative learning center in Drosophila brain.
source: The mushroom body is known to be the associative learning center in Drosophila brain (Heisenberg, 2003; McGuire et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Heisenberg, 2003 and McGuire et al., 2001.

claim: Mutation of the catalytic residue Asp298 to Asn (D298N) of CpOGA (CpOGACD) inactivates the enzymatic activity but retains its ability to bind O-GlcNAcylated peptides.
source: Mutation of the catalytic residue Asp298 to Asn (D298N) of CpOGA (CpOGACD) inactivates the enzymatic activity but retains its ability to bind O-GlcNAcylated peptides.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about CpOGA mutants.

claim: Immobilized CpOGACD has been successfully used to enrich O-GlcNAcylated substrates in vitro.
source: Taking advantage of this property, far western, gel electrophoresis, proximity ligation, and imaging methods have been developed (Selvan et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022; Song et al., 2021; Mariappa et al., 2015; Estevez et al., 2020), and immobilized CpOGACD has been successfully used to enrich O-GlcNAcylated substrates in vitro (Selvan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Selvan et al., 2017.

claim: Endogenous protein biotinylation level is low in most organisms including Drosophila.
source: Once induced by different tissue-specific drivers, this tool could tag and enrich O-GlcNAc substrates and their interactors in a tissue-specific manner, as endogenous protein biotinylation level is low in most organisms including Drosophila.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about endogenous biotinylation levels.

claim: 10 mM biotin treatment yielded robust biotinylation of proteins in HEK293T cells expressing TurboID-CpOGACD.
source: 10 mM biotin treatment yielded robust biotinylation of proteins, and this concentration was selected for subsequent experiments on cultured cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Thiamet-G increased global O-GlcNAcylation levels, and the overall biotinylation was consistently upregulated.
source: Thiamet-G increased global O-GlcNAcylation levels, and the overall biotinylation was consistently upregulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: OSMI-1 treatment decreased both O-GlcNAcylation and biotinylation in the cell lysates.
source: Conversely, OSMI-1 treatment decreased both O-GlcNAcylation and biotinylation in the cell lysates
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TurboID-CpOGACD effectively translates O-GlcNAc modification into biotin conjugation.
source: Conversely, OSMI-1 treatment decreased both O-GlcNAcylation and biotinylation in the cell lysates, suggesting that TurboID-CpOGACD effectively translates O-GlcNAc modification into biotin conjugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: TurboID-CpOGACD labeled more proteins with biotin in the input compared to TurboID-CpOGADM.
source: TurboID-CpOGACD labeled more proteins with biotin in the input compared to TurboID-CpOGADM, and consistently, more biotinylated proteins were immunoprecipitated.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Western blot with anti-O-GlcNAc antibody RL2 detected strong O-GlcNAcylation signals in immunoprecipitants from cells expressing TurboID-CpOGACD but not TurboID-CpOGADM.
source: Importantly, western blot with anti-O-GlcNAc antibody RL2 detected strong O-GlcNAcylation signals in immunoprecipitants from the cells expressing TurboID-CpOGACD but not TurboID-CpOGADM, indicating successful enrichment of O-GlcNAc substrates using the biotin tags (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The authors identified 336 O-GlcNAc candidate substrates from HEK293T cells.
source: We, therefore, identified 336 O-GlcNAc candidate substrates from HEK293T cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: 52% (178/336) of the O-GlcNAc candidate substrates identified in this study were also present in previous reports.
source: Overlap analysis revealed that 52% (178/336) of the O-GlcNAc candidate substrates identified in our study were also present in previous reports (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 48 proteins were shared among the three lists of O-GlcNAcylated proteins identified by different methods.
source: 48 proteins were shared among the three lists (Supplementary file 3), encompassing many well-known O-GlcNAcylated proteins such as OGT (Griffin et al., 2016), NUP153 (Li et al., 2022), NUP62 (Zhu et al., 2016), and HCFC1 (Capotosti et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Of the 158 candidate proteins that were unique in this study's result, 113 were annotated as O-GlcNAcylation substrates in the O-GlcNAc database.
source: Additionally, of the 158 candidate proteins that were unique in our result, 113 were annotated as O-GlcNAcylation substrates in the O-GlcNAc database (https://www.oglcnac.mcw.edu/).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with the O-GlcNAc database.

claim: TurboID-CpOGACD was able to selectively tag O-GlcNAcylated proteins with biotin for enrichment and identification.
source: These results validated that TurboID-CpOGACD was able to selectively tag O-GlcNAcylated proteins with biotin for enrichment and identification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments in HEK293T cells.

claim: TurboID-CpOGACD catalyzed more biotinylation in fly lysates relative to TurboID-CpOGADM.
source: Similar to the result with HEK293T cells, TurboID-CpOGACD catalyzed more biotinylation in the input relative to TurboID-CpOGADM, and more biotinylated proteins were immunoprecipitated, in which strong O-GlcNAcylation signals were detected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Staining with streptavidin-Cy3 detected strong biotinylation in the brain regions expressing TurboID-CpOGACD, whereas the rest of the brain showed negligible background signals.
source: More importantly, staining with streptavidin-Cy3 detected strong biotinylation in the brain regions expressing TurboID-CpOGACD, whereas the rest of the brain showed negligible background signals (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The authors identified 491 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in all neurons in the fly brain.
source: We, therefore, identified 491 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in all neurons in the fly brain (Elav-Gal4), 455 in the mushroom body (OK107-Gal4), 377 in the antennal lobe (GMR14H04-Gal4), 234 in the optic lobe (GMR33H10-Gal4), and 289 in the ellipsoid body (c232-Gal4) (Figure 3D, Supplementary files 4-8).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The authors identified 455 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in the mushroom body.
source: We, therefore, identified 491 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in all neurons in the fly brain (Elav-Gal4), 455 in the mushroom body (OK107-Gal4), 377 in the antennal lobe (GMR14H04-Gal4), 234 in the optic lobe (GMR33H10-Gal4), and 289 in the ellipsoid body (c232-Gal4) (Figure 3D, Supplementary files 4-8).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The authors identified 377 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in the antennal lobe.
source: We, therefore, identified 491 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in all neurons in the fly brain (Elav-Gal4), 455 in the mushroom body (OK107-Gal4), 377 in the antennal lobe (GMR14H04-Gal4), 234 in the optic lobe (GMR33H10-Gal4), and 289 in the ellipsoid body (c232-Gal4) (Figure 3D, Supplementary files 4-8).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The authors identified 234 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in the optic lobe.
source: We, therefore, identified 491 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in all neurons in the fly brain (Elav-Gal4), 455 in the mushroom body (OK107-Gal4), 377 in the antennal lobe (GMR14H04-Gal4), 234 in the optic lobe (GMR33H10-Gal4), and 289 in the ellipsoid body (c232-Gal4) (Figure 3D, Supplementary files 4-8).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The authors identified 289 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in the ellipsoid body.
source: We, therefore, identified 491 putative O-GlcNAcylated proteins in all neurons in the fly brain (Elav-Gal4), 455 in the mushroom body (OK107-Gal4), 377 in the antennal lobe (GMR14H04-Gal4), 234 in the optic lobe (GMR33H10-Gal4), and 289 in the ellipsoid body (c232-Gal4) (Figure 3D, Supplementary files 4-8).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The O-GlcNAc interactome in brain neurons was enriched in chemical synaptic transmission, neurotransmitter secretion, as well as chromatin remodeling.
source: The O-GlcNAc interactome in brain neurons was enriched in chemical synaptic transmission, neurotransmitter secretion, as well as chromatin remodeling
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Putative O-GlcNAcylation modifications in the mushroom body were highly clustered in processes linked to translation, including cytoplasmic translation, translational initiation, ribosome assembly, and ribosome biogenesis.
source: Of particular interest, putative O-GlcNAcylation modifications in the mushroom body were highly clustered in processes linked to translation, including cytoplasmic translation, translational initiation, ribosome assembly, and ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Nearly 10% of the putative O-GlcNAc substrates in the mushroom body were from ribosomes, much higher than that in other brain regions.
source: We calculated the percentage of ribosomal components in all the proteins identified from different brain regions, and found that nearly 10% of the putative O-GlcNAc substrates in the mushroom body were from ribosomes, much higher than that in other brain regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: While the O-GlcNAc levels of ribosomal proteins were highest in the mushroom body, their mRNA abundances were not.
source: While the O-GlcNAc levels were highest in the mushroom body, their mRNA abundances were not (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the mushroom body, the O-GlcNAc levels of ribosomal proteins showed no correlation with their mRNA abundances.
source: Moreover, in the mushroom body, the O-GlcNAc levels of these ribosomal proteins showed no correlation with their mRNA abundances (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ribosomes purified from mushroom body contained more O-GlcNAc modifications than that from whole brain neurons.
source: Western blot with anti-O-GlcNAc antibody RL2 showed that ribosomes purified from mushroom body contained more O-GlcNAc modifications than that from whole brain neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ribosomal components were abundantly O-GlcNAc modified in the learning center of Drosophila brain.
